reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Faciobrachial dystonic seizures — brief, frequent unilateral contractions of the face and arm — are highly characteristic and often precede the cognitive syndrome
The limbic phase brings subacute short-term memory loss, confusion, temporal-lobe seizures, and disturbed sleep or behaviour
Hyponatraemia is common and helps raise suspicion of the diagnosis
Antibodies target LGI1, a secreted neuronal protein once grouped within the voltage-gated potassium channel complex
Most cases are non-paraneoplastic, but tumour screening remains appropriate as a minority harbour an underlying neoplasm
Recognising and treating faciobrachial dystonic seizures early with immunotherapy may prevent progression to fixed cognitive impairment
First-line immunotherapy is corticosteroids with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, escalating to rituximab in refractory disease
reference.pathophysiology: Antibodies are directed against leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1 (LGI1), a protein secreted by neurons that bridges presynaptic ADAM23 and postsynaptic ADAM22 to regulate synaptic excitability and AMPA-receptor clustering. Antibody-mediated disruption of this signalling increases neuronal excitability within the temporal lobes and basal ganglia, producing seizures, and impairs limbic circuits underlying memory. Inflammation concentrates in the medial temporal structures, and associated hypothalamic involvement is thought to contribute to the frequent hyponatraemia. The response is usually not tumour-driven but is strongly linked to specific HLA types.
additionalDifferentials: Herpes simplex and other infective limbic encephalitis
Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis with intracellular antibodies
Rapidly progressive dementia including Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid testing for LGI1 antibodies, with serum often more sensitive for this antigen
MRI of the brain showing medial temporal and sometimes basal ganglia signal change
Electroencephalography to characterise temporal seizures and subclinical activity
Serum sodium measurement to detect hyponatraemia
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for inflammation and to exclude infection
Targeted tumour screening given the small paraneoplastic association
redFlags: Frequent faciobrachial dystonic seizures signalling active, treatable disease before cognitive decline
Rapidly progressive memory loss or confusion
Severe hyponatraemia risking seizures and reduced consciousness
reference.prognosis: Prompt immunotherapy often improves seizures and cognition, but delayed treatment is associated with persistent memory impairment and medial temporal atrophy. Relapses can occur, so ongoing monitoring is warranted.
pitfalls: Mistaking faciobrachial dystonic seizures for tics, myoclonus, or psychogenic movements and delaying treatment
Relying on antiseizure drugs alone rather than starting immunotherapy
Overlooking hyponatraemia as a diagnostic clue
Assuming the disorder is always non-paraneoplastic and omitting tumour screening
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: First-line immunotherapy with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin and/or plasma exchange
Second-line immunotherapy with rituximab or cyclophosphamide for refractory or relapsing disease
Early immunotherapy for faciobrachial dystonic seizures to prevent progression to fixed cognitive impairment, with antiseizure medication as adjunct
Tumour screening despite the mostly non-paraneoplastic nature, treating any identified neoplasm
Cognitive rehabilitation and management of sleep and behavioural disturbance
Clinical and antibody follow-up to detect relapse, under neurology and neuroimmunology multidisciplinary care
